run.userPrompt:
A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentResponses.content:
**Start where nobody wants to: the margin claim.**

"Higher margins" is the part of this that gets asserted and never modelled. We hand a retailer 30-odd points and they absorb the returns, the payment fees, the pick-and-pack, the customer who calls twice, the acquisition of the customer in the first place, and the working capital. Load all of that back onto our own P&L at the volumes a new web store actually does in year one, and the contribution per unit is frequently *worse* than wholesale — and it stays worse until scale arrives, which it does slowly and expensively.

This matters more than it sounds, because it determines what the channel becomes. If direct is chartered on a margin thesis, it will be given a revenue number. Given a revenue number, it will discount, promote, and run paid search on our own brand terms — and it will do all three by month five, because that's the only lever a small channel has. That is precisely the behaviour that starts the war. **A direct business built to make money in two years will pick a fight it cannot win. A direct business built to acquire identity and obligation will not have to.**

So the honest case for this is the first-party relationship, the consumables and service annuity that hangs off it, and the option value of not having 55% of our revenue inside two phone calls. That's a strong enough case. We should stop dressing it in a margin story that finance will eventually audit.

---

**And the sentence I'd interrogate second: "have punished suppliers who competed with them directly."**

Punished how, specifically, to whom, and what did it cost? Facings, promo exclusion, delisting, terms renegotiation, or a hard delist of the whole line? These are wildly different weapons and we appear to be treating them as one. Someone can reconstruct three or four case histories in a fortnight — those stories circulate in every category, and half of them are folklore attached to a supplier who was also failing on fill rate or had lost a competitive line review on the merits.

What I want is a number: the P&L consequence of losing two facings and one seasonal promotion at each of the two, modelled honestly. Because that number is our risk budget for everything that follows. Right now we're negotiating with an imagined penalty of infinite size, which is the same as having no strategy at all.

**Then the angry call itself, which is data and is being read as a verdict.** Who rang — the buyer, or their director? And what did they actually object to? In my experience the words are about the web store and the injury is about *finding out from someone else*. A buyer's compensation is sell-through in their doors; their standing internally rests on not being surprised in front of their own boss. If the substance of that call was "you undercut my price" we have one problem. If it was "why am I hearing this from a customer" we have an entirely different and much cheaper one, and the remedy is a briefing calendar rather than a channel strategy.

I'd find out which. It changes everything downstream.

---

## Channel architecture: the direct channel should not be a store

The reflex is a website that sells our products. That is the one design guaranteed to produce conflict, because it creates a matched pair — same UPC, same picture, two prices — and a buyer whose job is to notice matched pairs.

Build instead a **direct estate with four rooms, only one of which sells anything a retailer stocks.**

**1. The registration and service layer — where the data actually lives.**
Data does not require a transaction. It requires a reason for the customer to identify themselves. Extended warranty on registration. Manuals, spares diagrams, how-to. Replacement parts and consumables. Service booking. This layer captures the buyer *of the retailer's unit* — legitimately, visibly, and with the retailer's blessing, because it reduces their return rate and their call volume. Ninety percent of what management wants from "first-party data" is available here without selling a single competing box.

**2. The endless aisle.** Every colour, size, configuration, and long-tail variant no buyer will ever give shelf space to. This is not competition; it is the recovery of demand the retailer has already declined to serve. It also gives us the single most useful sentence in the partner conversation: *we sell direct only what you have chosen not to carry.*

**3. Direct-only architecture.** Configured, personalised, made-to-order, bundled, gifted, subscribed. Distinct names, distinct packs, no comparable barcode. A subscription or replenishment relationship is structurally uncomparable — there is no shelf price to sit next to. And made-to-order carries a lead time, which is itself a defence: nobody standing in an aisle is our customer for a four-week configurable.

**4. The take-back and trade-in room.** We want the old unit and the identity that comes with it.

The governing rule, published internally and never quietly relaxed: **no SKU appears at retail and direct in the same form at a different net price.** Not similar. The same.

---

## The move that converts the threat into a gift: give them the sale

Here is the part I'd push hardest, and it will be unpopular with whoever owns the DTC P&L.

Put a **"buy from your retailer"** path on every product page — real inventory, real store locator, real click-through, and where the partner's systems permit it, **direct orders routed to them for fulfilment and revenue credit**. We keep the customer record, the consent, the service relationship, the replenishment. They book the sale.

Read the arithmetic honestly: we've given away the margin we were told was the point, and kept the thing that was actually the point. And we've turned a channel our partners were told to fear into a demand-generation asset with an attributable number on it — units and revenue *we sent them*, reported monthly, in their format.

That number is the currency of every subsequent conversation. A supplier arguing about channel rights loses. A supplier who arrives with "we drove 8,400 units into your doors last quarter, here they are by store" is having a different meeting entirely.

---

## Pricing: hold the umbrella, don't undercut it

Direct price sits **at or above** shelf, permanently, contractually, publicly. We never win a customer on price in our own channel. We win on assortment, configuration, service, access, and the fact that we answer the phone.

Value flows to the direct customer through things that cannot be photographed and set beside a shelf tag: warranty extension, included service, bundled consumables, a loyalty credit redeemable against the *next* purchase — which the buyer's price-comparison scrape does not see and cannot object to, and which builds a repeat behaviour a retailer cannot capture anyway.

And the concession that costs us nothing and is worth more than three points of trade spend: **become the enforcer of our own pricing.** Publish a minimum-advertised-price policy with teeth, and then use it — on grey-market resellers, unauthorised marketplace sellers, the liquidator dumping last season's stock at 40% off in the same search results the buyer's team monitors. That chaos is the thing retail buyers genuinely hate about us, and it isn't our direct store, it's the eleven anonymous sellers no one is policing. Cleaning that up buys credibility that no amount of promotional funding will.

I'd be curious whether either buying team, asked directly and privately, would rank our web store above the marketplace mess as their actual grievance. My guess is no, and I'd rather find that out by asking than by inferring.

---

## Data strategy: consent, then reciprocity

**Acquire it with an exchange, not a checkbox.** Registration for warranty, replenishment for convenience, app for function, service history for peace of mind. Every one of those is a reason a customer volunteers identity, and every one works on units bought at retail. The installed base is the asset — not the transaction log.

**Build for identity, not attribution.** One record per household, unified across registration, service, consumables, and direct purchase. The goal is a durable relationship with the end user, not a marketing funnel.

**Then be conspicuously generous with what we learn.** This is the counterintuitive part and I'd hold it as policy: share back to partners what they cannot compute themselves — cross-retailer category demand signals, returns reason codes at SKU level, why-they-didn't-buy research, regional demand forecasting by store cluster, demographic and use-case profiles. We sit above both retailers and see the category whole; neither of them can see the other's shelf.

A supplier who arrives quarterly with insight the buyer can take to their own line review becomes structurally hard to punish, because punishing us costs them something specific and personal. That is a better defence than any clause we could negotiate. Where their governance allows it, a clean-room arrangement formalises the exchange and does more for the relationship than a decade of trade allowances.

What we do *not* do is use their sell-through data to target their customers off their shelf. Once. Ever. That's the one breach from which there is no recovery, and it will be tempting to a young growth team measured on CAC. Whoever runs direct should be told this in the first week, and should carry partner-relationship health in their compensation rather than direct revenue.

---

## The partner-communication plan

The organising principle is one sentence: **no partner ever learns about our direct activity from a customer, a competitor's rep, or their own scrape.**

- **Pre-brief, at their director level, before anything is live** — above the buyer, so the buyer is protected rather than ambushed, and framed as a full-line availability and demand-generation programme with a store-locator commitment. Not as strategy. Certainly not as transformation.
- **Bring them the assortment protection first.** Hero SKUs and new launches exclusive to their floor, in writing, with a first-window on introductions. Direct gets the tail and the configurables. That trade is worth more to a buyer than the concession they think they want, because it's defensible internally.
- **Give the buyer something to take upstairs.** A referred-units number, a returns-reduction number, a joint calendar. Buyers aren't obstacles; they're people with a scorecard, and we know most of what's on it.
- **A single named relationship owner per partner, senior, who does not report to whoever owns direct.** The structural failure here is one person carrying both a DTC growth target and a partner relationship, and everyone can predict which one gets sacrificed in a bad quarter.
- **Quarterly, unprompted, in advance of being asked**: what we're doing direct, what we're launching, what we referred them, what we've taken down. Predictability is the entire product. A partner who can forecast our behaviour will tolerate a surprising amount of it.
- **And nothing about "DTC" in any document that could leave the building.** Not because it's dishonest — the substance is exactly as described — but because the label triggers a reflex that the substance does not. If a slide is titled *Direct-to-Consumer Strategy*, it will eventually be photographed. Call it what it functionally is: consumer registration, full-line availability, service and consumables.

---

## What I'd test this quarter, cheaply

- **Reconstruct the punishment cases** and model the cost of losing two facings and a promotion at each of the two. That number is the risk budget for the whole programme.
- **Diagnose the angry call properly.** Surprise, or price? One is a calendar problem. Ask the buyer directly, informally, off the record. They will tell us.
- **Registration and warranty-extension capture on retail-bought units, one product family.** No commerce at all. Measure opt-in rate. If we can't get identity when we're giving something away and competing with nobody, the commercial version was never going to work either, and we'll have learned that for the price of a landing page.
- **True direct contribution margin at realistic volumes** — CAC, returns, payments, fulfilment, service, all loaded. Publish it before anyone builds a plan on the wholesale-discount fantasy.
- **A consumables or replenishment offer**, quietly, one region. Structurally uncomparable, and it tells us whether a repeat relationship exists at all.
- **An unauthorised-seller sweep**, with the results shown to both buying teams. Costs almost nothing, and I suspect it's the highest-return goodwill purchase available to us.
- **Store-locator referral instrumentation**, live now, so that when the difficult conversation comes we have six months of numbers rather than an argument.

---

## Sequencing

Registration, service, parts and content immediately — no commerce, no conflict, and it takes the longest to accumulate. Pre-briefing and the assortment-protection trade before anything transacts, not after. Endless-aisle and configurables at three to six months, positioned as recovery of declined demand. MAP enforcement and the insight-sharing rhythm in parallel, because both buy credibility and neither requires anyone's permission. Subscription and consumables at six to nine. Retailer-fulfilled direct routing wherever their systems allow, as early as they'll take it. Distinct direct-only architecture at twelve-plus, and only if the registration numbers earned it.

Underneath all of it, quietly: **partner concentration is the actual disease.** Direct is one hedge and a slow one. Independents, professional and specification channels, international, adjacent formats — a third partner at 8% changes the tone of a negotiation more than a website ever will. Nobody has asked for that workstream, and I'd start it anyway.

---

**And the question that isn't mine to settle.** Are we building a channel or a relationship? Because if it's the relationship — the installed base, the consent, the service book, the replenishment — then we can have almost all of it without ever putting a competing price in front of those two buyers, and the fight everyone is braced for simply doesn't need to happen. If it's genuinely the channel, with a revenue line and a growth target attached, then we are choosing a war over 55% of revenue and we should say so plainly, resource it as a war, and know what we'll do in the quarter after the delisting.

I'd want that settled before the first registration numbers arrive, because once they do, everyone will read them as proof of whatever they already wanted.

I'll begin with the punishment-case reconstruction and the registration test. Neither requires a decision from anyone, and one of them will tell us how much room we actually have.
